title: Event-related potentials to alcohol images predict real-world collegiate binge drinking: a pilot study of “lab-to-life” associations using wearable alcohol biosensors
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Event-related potentials (ERPs) are described as neural markers of risk for hazardous drinking, but few studies have related “lab to life” by linking ERPs to temporally-sensitive measures of real-world drinking. We predicted that ERPs reflecting alcohol cue-reactivity (ACR) and inhibitory control (AIC) would correlate with real-world transdermal alcohol concentrations (TACs) measured via alcohol biosensor. Methods: College binge drinkers (N = 27; Mage = 21.2; 67% female) completed a two-condition alcohol Go/No-Go task, then wore a SCRAMx biosensor for 12 days. Partial correlations examined the relationships between drinking (retrospective self-reports, ecological momentary assessments, and TACs) and ERPs to alcohol images, controlling for control images. ERPs to alcohol Go trials indexed ACR. ERPs to alcohol No-Go trials reflected AIC. Results: Shorter N2 latencies to alcohol Go, reflecting higher ACR, were associated with faster TAC rise rate, signaling faster alcohol absorption and intoxication. Larger, more prolonged N2s to alcohol No-Go, reflecting lower AIC, were associated with greater average TAC, peak TAC, and area under the TAC curve, indicating a greater alcohol consumption volume. P3s were larger and more prolonged to NoGo versus Go; no other relationships were significant. Conclusion: This is the first study to include wearable alcohol biosensors in an ERP-related, lab-to-life design. Findings substantiate associations between ERPs and real-world drinking. While enhanced ACR may spark a drinking episode, impaired AIC may allow it to escalate into a binge. Objective, temporally-sensitive TACs may provide targets for ecological momentary interventions to disrupt the speed of intoxication and the magnitude of drinking episodes.
